Catholics who refused to attend Anglican services faced heavy fines after 1581, while missionary priests such as Edmund Campion were executed as traitors.
Elizabeth ruled through her court, a Privy Council guided by ministers such as William Cecil (Lord Burghley), and occasional Parliaments.
The Catholic claimant held captive in England; evidence of her involvement in the Babington Plot led to her execution at Fotheringhay in 1587.
Rising population and the terrible harvests of the 1590s increased vagrancy, and the 1601 Poor Law made each parish responsible for its own poor.
Philip II's invasion fleet was scattered by English fireships at Calais and shattered by storms as it fled around Scotland and Ireland.
A flourishing of drama, music and exploration, with playhouses such as the Globe (1599) and voyagers like Drake, although life stayed harsh for most people.
Confrontations such as Hungary 1956, the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961 and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 brought repeated danger of war.
Arms control agreements like SALT 1 and the Helsinki Accords eased tension until the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 triggered a 'Second Cold War'.
Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika, the 1989 revolutions in Eastern Europe and the fall of the Berlin Wall preceded the dissolution of the USSR in 1991.
The wartime partnership of the USA, USSR and Britain against the Axis, strained at Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam by disputes over Eastern Europe.
Between 1945 and 1949 the Iron Curtain, Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Berlin Blockade and creation of NATO divided Europe into rival blocs.
After 1991 the USA stood as sole superpower; the 9/11 attacks of 2001 led to wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, while Russia grew more assertive by 2010.
The Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, banning of parties and the Night of the Long Knives made Hitler Führer of a one-party state by 1934.
Persecution escalated from the 1933 boycott through the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and Kristallnacht in 1938 to ghettos and the Holocaust during the war.
Goebbels's ministry controlled newspapers, cheap 'people's receiver' radios, film and mass rallies such as Nuremberg to spread the Hitler myth.
The SS and Gestapo, helped by informers and concentration camps, crushed opposition, while courts and judges were brought under Nazi control.
War brought rationing, bombing and total mobilisation, and resistance grew from groups like the White Rose to the July 1944 bomb plot.
The Hitler Youth and League of German Maidens trained boys for war and girls for motherhood, while school subjects were rewritten around race and loyalty.

the-peoples-health-c1250-to-present.d: The People's Health c1250 to Present
terms: Plague killed around a third or more of England's population; responses included prayer, flight, quarantine attempts and blaming bad air.
During London's last major plague outbreak, infected households were shut up and marked with red crosses, searchers counted the dead, and victims were buried in plague pits.
Rapid urban growth created slums with foul water, and cholera epidemics repeatedly struck Britain from 1831-32 onwards.
Overcrowded streets, shared wells, cesspits and butchers' waste threatened health; town authorities issued sanitation rules but enforcement was weak.
Chadwick's 1842 report, John Snow's 1854 Broad Street pump study, Bazalgette's sewers and the Public Health Acts of 1848 and 1875 transformed towns.
The Liberal reforms of 1906-11, council housing and the creation of the NHS in 1948 made government responsible for the people's health.
